rows.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in Leslie's argument?

steps.body: Your quest for the treasure is irrational.
steps.label: Conclusion

steps.body: You would not sacrifice one of your hands in order to possess the world. Your hands are more important than possessing the world. Your entire body is necessarily more important to you than your hands. You are ruining your health and harming your body in your quest for a treasure that is much less valuable than the whole world.
steps.label: Evidence

rows.stimulus: Leslie: I'll show you that your quest for the treasure is irrational. Suppose you found a tablet inscribed, "Whoever touches this tablet will lose a hand, yet will possess the world." Would you touch it? Erich: Certainly not. Leslie: Just as I expected! It is clear from your answer that your hands are more important to you than possessing the world. But your entire body is necessarily more important to you than your hands. Yet you are ruining your health and harming your body in your quest for a treasure that is much less valuable than the whole world. I rest my case.

notes.body: B also takes road 1. The warmer discharge sends bass off to find cooler water elsewhere. Fewer bass stay downstream of the plant, so anglers there catch fewer. That explains the drop, so eliminate B.

E is road 1 again. Turbulence from the wastewater disrupted the river vegetation and destroyed some of the bass's habitat. Less habitat supports fewer bass downstream, so fewer get caught. E explains the drop.

D is the road 2 answer, and it is easy to throw out as off topic because it is about anglers, not bass. The bass may be fine. But noise makes that stretch of river a less popular place to fish, and fewer anglers catch fewer bass. That is exactly the decrease described, so D explains it and is out.

C pushes the other way. Better access brings more anglers fishing for bass downstream. More people fishing should mean more bass caught, not fewer, so C cannot explain the decrease.

Could you rescue C by imagining the extra anglers fished the bass out? Only by inventing that story yourself, and it runs against what C actually tells us. C's own effect is more people fishing, and on its face that means more bass caught. The four other answers each point straight at fewer bass caught; C points the other way. That is what marks the answer that does not belong.
A takes road 1. If the wastewater draws in fish that prey on bass, more bass get eaten and fewer are left downstream to catch. That explains the drop in bass caught, so A is out.

rows.prompt: Each of the following, if true, could explain the decrease described above EXCEPT:

steps.body: The power plant opened and started discharging wastewater into the river.
steps.label: Given that ...

steps.body:
This isn't a true paradox. Nothing here is surprising. The stem just wants explanations for a drop in the number of bass caught.

Think about what "number of bass caught" depends on. It takes two things: bass in the water and people fishing for them. So there are two roads to fewer bass caught:
1. **Fewer bass downstream.** They died, got eaten, moved away, or lost their habitat.
2. **Less fishing downstream.** Fewer anglers, or anglers fishing less.

Expect most of the answers we eliminate to come in on road 1, with at least one sneaking in on road 2.

Most students only think of road 1, because the wastewater feels like it must be hurting the fish. But road 2 is just as good. If half the anglers stop showing up, half as many bass get caught, even if the bass are thriving.
steps.label: Evaluate

steps.body:
Eliminate four answers that explain fewer bass caught, by either road. The correct answer will do neither, or it will push the other way: more bass or more fishing, which should mean *more* bass caught.

Be careful with any answer about anglers. It isn't out of scope. Anglers are half the equation.
steps.label: Goal

steps.body: Shortly after, anglers downstream caught fewer bass overall?
steps.label: Why is it that ...

rows.stimulus: Shortly after the power plant opened and began discharging its wastewater into the river, there was a decrease in the overall number of bass caught by anglers downstream from the plant.

notes.body: This compares sewage pollution with pollution "in some other way." The stimulus never mentions any other kind of pollution, so we have nothing to compare against. Even for sewage, the fish kill only happens "sometimes," so we can't rank sewage as the deadlier pollutant.

The stimulus describes one way sewage can harm fish: the algae it produces feed microorganisms that are toxic to fish. It never rules out other kinds of harm, so saying sewage does not harm fish "in any way other than" this one goes too far.

The stimulus says the algae give toxic microorganisms "a rich food source." It says nothing about how fast those microorganisms reproduce or how they compare with other microorganisms. Plenty of food for one group doesn't prove that group outgrows all the others.

This connects the first cause to the final effect: sewage overnutrifies the water, the water grows algae, and the algae sometimes feed microorganisms that kill most of the fish.

The word "can" is what makes it safe. Because the last link only happens "sometimes," the chain proves possibility, not certainty. When a chain has a weak link, the right answer keeps that weakness in its wording.

Sewage pollution is one way to get algae to proliferate. Nothing says it's the only way. D treats a cause as a requirement. Test it: an estuary with no sewage that gets nutrients from farm runoff could still fill with algae, and nothing in the stimulus says otherwise.

rows.prompt: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the information above?

steps.body: Look for a softly worded answer that joins the start of the chain to the end: overnutrifying an estuary with sewage can lead to most of its fish dying. An answer that says this "will" happen goes past the "sometimes".
steps.label: Goal

steps.body:
Coastal estuaries are easily polluted by nutrient-rich sewage.

When that pollution overnutrifies the water, algae proliferate.
sewage overnutrifies water → algae proliferate

The abundant algae "sometimes" feed microorganisms that are toxic to fish, killing most of the fish.
abundant algae → (sometimes) toxic microorganisms thrive → most fish die
steps.label: Given

steps.body:
Each sentence picks up where the last one ended: sewage leads to overnutrified water, overnutrified water leads to algae, and algae can lead to a fish kill. When causes and effects line up end to end like this, connect the first cause to the last effect.

Watch the word "sometimes" on the last link. The algae don't always feed toxic microorganisms. So the chain doesn't prove that sewage always kills the fish. It proves that it can.
steps.label: Evaluate

rows.stimulus: The calm, shallow waters of coastal estuaries are easily polluted by nutrient-rich sewage. When estuary waters become overnutrified as a result, algae proliferate. The abundant algae, in turn, sometimes provide a rich food source for microorganisms that are toxic to fish, thereby killing most of the fish in the estuary.

notes.body:
The author doesn't need to assume that Astorga sought out opinion polls because she has no strong opinions of her own.

She may well have strong opinions but still seek opinion polls to see how well they align with the strong opinions of voters.

Furthermore, she may have strong opinions of what she thinks the new mayor ought to do, while still hiding those opinions and just telling the voters what they want to hear.

So negating this, and saying "she does have at least one strong opinion" wouldn't weaken the argument at all.

The argument is only about whether Astorga's intent matches her current rhetoric. The argument isn't affected one way or the other by whether Astorga wins or loses the election, so the author doesn't need to assume anything about what votes she'll receive or not receive.

Furthermore, the word/concept of "most" will be wrong on Necessary Assumption 99.5% of the time we see it. When you negate "most" you're basically saying, "Nuh-uh, author. It's not true that at least 51% of voters are unlikely to be persuaded. It's at most 49%."

No argument is ever badly weakened by switching from "at least 51%" to "at most 49%", so negating "most" will basically never weaken.

The author didn't indicate any skepticism of the opinion polls. He may well believe that the opinion polls correctly reflect the voters' actual wishlist, but still believe that Astorga has no plans to actually follow through on these campaign promises (she's just telling voters what they want to hear in order to get elected).

This just establishes the difference that the author was assuming.

Astorga is telling voters that she'll do the things she knows they want the mayor to do. The author believes that voters aren't hearing what she'll really do.

So the author is assuming that she won't really do the things she knows they want the mayor to do.

If we negated this answer, we'd get, "Astorga actually does intend, if elected, to do [the things she's currently telling voters that she intends to do]", which would badly weaken the argument by essentially contradicting the conclusion.

The argument is about Intent, not results / capacity / feasibility. The author doesn't have to assume that Astorga is incapable of following through on her campaign promises.

He might believe that she's perfectly capable of following through on the promises, but just doesn't plan to because she's not willing to pursue those ends.

rows.prompt: Which one of the following is a questionable assumption on which the argument relies?

steps.body: Astorga is telling voters that, if she becomes mayor, she'll do [all the things she's learned from opinion polls that voters want the new mayor to do].
steps.label: Evidence

steps.body: Voters aren't being told what Astorga really plans to do if she becomes mayor.
steps.label: Conclusion

steps.body:
Look for an answer establishing the "assumed difference" -- i.e., Astorga doesn't intend to do the stuff she's currently telling voters that she'll do.
Or look for an answer that the author is clearly committed to thinking, something that, if negated, would badly weaken his argument.
steps.label: Goal

steps.body:
How did the author think he proved that voters aren't really hearing what Astorga plans to do? This is a Comparison argument in which the author is assuming a difference.
The author assumes that what Astorga plans to do is different from what she's currently telling voters she'll do.
She seems to be cynically thinking that Astorga has her own plans for being mayor, and she is just looking at opinion polls and disingenuously lying to voters, acting like she's going to work on their wishlist, but she's really just saying that stuff to get elected, and then will proceed with her "real" agenda.
steps.label: Evaluate

rows.stimulus: Astorga’s campaign promises are apparently just an attempt to please voters. What she says she will do if elected mayor is simply what she has learned from opinion polls that voters want the new mayor to do. Therefore, voters are not being told what Astorga actually intends to do if she becomes mayor.

notes.body: If most low-melting-point medications are soft-gels, that points M toward a form this company can't make. It gives no reason to think M ends up as a capsule, and it never puts M under the unpleasant-taste rule.

This is the missing trigger. With M tasting unpleasant, the first premise applies: M will generally come as a tablet, capsule, or soft-gel. The heat rules out tablet, the company's missing technology rules out soft-gel, and capsule is what remains.
PT → (T or C or SG)
PT, ~T, ~SG, so C

The move: when an argument eliminates options from a rule, check that the rule actually applies to the thing in the conclusion.

If M can be made as a liquid, that adds a fourth option outside tablet, capsule, and soft-gel. That makes capsule less certain, not more. It also does nothing to show that M tastes unpleasant, so the three-option rule still isn't triggered.

This says a capsule medication isn't also a soft-gel (C → ~SG). We already know M won't be a soft-gel, so this adds nothing. And it still doesn't tell us M is limited to the three forms, because nothing says M tastes unpleasant.

This gives a reason to choose capsules for bad-tasting medicine, but it only matters if M tastes bad. E never says it does. Without that, M isn't covered by the rule and could be produced in a form outside the three listed.

rows.prompt: The conclusion is most strongly supported by the reasoning in the argument if which one of the following is assumed?

steps.body:
Medications with an unpleasant taste are generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form.
PT → (T or C or SG)

The active ingredient in medication M is a waxy substance that cannot tolerate the heat used to manufacture tablets because it has a low melting point.
~T

The company developing M does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology and manufactures all its medications itself.
~SG
steps.label: Evidence

steps.body: The stem says "if which one of the following is assumed", so we want the piece that makes the conclusion follow. The missing piece is the rule's trigger: M has an unpleasant taste. Once that's in place, the three-option rule applies, two options are gone, and capsule is the one left.
steps.label: Goal

steps.body:
M will most likely be produced in capsule form.
C
steps.label: Conclusion

steps.body:
The conclusion follows a process of elimination. Medications with an unpleasant taste are "generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form." M can't be a tablet, because its waxy ingredient can't take the heat. M can't be a soft-gel, because the company "does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology" and makes everything itself. Capsule is what's left.

But look at who the first rule covers: only medications with an unpleasant taste. Nothing tells us M tastes bad. If M tastes fine, the rule never applies, and M could come in a liquid, a powder, or anything else. The elimination only works if M is in the group the rule covers.
PT → (T or C or SG)
~T
~SG
missing: PT
steps.label: Evaluate

rows.stimulus: Medications with an unpleasant taste are generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form. The active ingredient in medication M is a waxy substance that cannot tolerate the heat used to manufacture tablets because it has a low melting point. So, since the company developing M does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology and manufactures all its medications itself, M will most likely be produced in capsule form.

notes.body: B is too strong. The argument can allow that some dishes do better with faster cooking. It only says that when a bean dish's quality matters more than speed, the beans shouldn't be presoaked.
The argument is only about whether to presoak the beans. It needs no claim about whether anything else in the dish gets presoaked.

This is the link from the Evaluate step. Negate it: plumper beans do not enhance the quality of a dish. Then skipping the soak buys nothing on the quality side, and the conclusion has no support.

The pattern to repeat: find the idea that appears only in the conclusion (quality), find the idea it replaced in the evidence (plumper beans), and look for the answer that connects them.

E links plumpness to taste, but the conclusion is about a dish's quality. The argument doesn't need plumpness to work through taste: plumper beans could improve a dish's quality even if they taste no better.
The argument never compares appearance with taste. Plumper beans could improve a dish for any reason, so the argument doesn't need appearance to be as important as taste.

rows.prompt: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

steps.body: Therefore, when a bean dish's quality is more important than the need to cook that dish quickly, beans should not be presoaked.
steps.label: Conclusion

steps.body:
The evidence gives a trade-off. Presoaking saves time. Skipping it gives plumper beans. The conclusion says that when quality matters more than speed, skip the soak.

Notice the jump. The evidence talks about plumper beans. The conclusion talks about the dish's quality. Those aren't the same idea. How could we argue against the author? Suppose plumper beans don't make a dish any better. Then the only real difference between the two methods is cooking time, and there's no quality reason to skip the soak.

So the author has to assume that plumper beans make for a better dish.
steps.label: Evaluate

steps.body:
Soaking dried beans overnight before cooking them reduces cooking time.
However, cooking without presoaking yields plumper beans.
steps.label: Evidence

steps.body: Look for an answer that links plumper beans to a better dish. When the conclusion brings in an idea the evidence never mentioned (quality), the gap is usually the link between the evidence's idea and that new one. Confirm it with the negation test: if plumper beans do nothing for a dish, the argument falls apart.
steps.label: Goal

rows.stimulus: Soaking dried beans overnight before cooking them reduces cooking time. However, cooking without presoaking yields plumper beans. Therefore, when a bean dish's quality is more important than the need to cook that dish quickly, beans should not be presoaked.

notes.body:
We're trying to explain why a raisin has more iron per calorie than the grape it formed from.

The paradox is only about the chemistry of the grape/raisin. It has nothing to do with organisms that consume grapes or raisins. So it's irrelevant how a grape or raisin interacts with a human body.

This is offering us a story of how a grape sheds calories en route to being a raisin.

The grape had 20mg of iron and 10 calories. **2 mg iron per calorie**

The raisin keeps that 20mg of iron. "The only thing removed from the grapes is water".

But the sugar in the grape caramelizes as it becomes a raisin. And when we measure how many calories something has, we don't count calories in caramelized sugar (because the body can't digest it).

So when we measure the raisin that formed from that 10 calorie grape, we get a number lower than 10.

Some of the grape's 10 calories were from sugar. When that sugar caramelized, then those sugar-calories stop being counted.

If there were 3 calories from the sugar, then now that the grape has caramelized into a raisin, that 10 calorie grape will only be a 7 calorie raisin.

And if the raisin has 20mg of iron and is only 7 calories, then it's close to being **3 mg iron per calorie**.

So this answer allows us to explain why a raisin made from a given grape can have more iron per calorie than the grape, even though no iron is added and only water is removed.

This reinforces the fact that raisins are more iron-rich than grapes (you'd only need a handful of raisins to get the same iron you'd get out of eating several bunches of grapes).

But it doesn't explain **why** raisins are more iron-rich than grapes.

We're trying to explain why a raisin has more iron per calorie than the grape from which it was formed.

The paradox is only about the chemistry of the grape/raisin. It has nothing to do with any other foods you might later mix with raisins or grapes. This answer feels like a correct answer, because it feels like we're offering an alternate explanation for why raisins seem to have more iron than grapes. ("It's not because raisins are inherently more iron-heavy, it's just that they're eaten with other foods that supply iron.")

But we are accepting as a given the fact that raisins are more iron-heavy than grapes. We need to explain why they are so.

This reinforces the fact that raisins are more iron-rich than grapes (people get more of their yearly iron from raisins than from grapes).

But it doesn't explain **why** raisins are more iron-rich than grapes.

rows.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why raisins contain more iron per calorie than do grapes?

steps.body: Since there's no way to add more iron, we want an answer to talk to us about how going from a grape to a raisin sheds calories.
steps.label: Goal

steps.body: Raisins are made from grapes, and nothing is added in the process,
steps.label: Given that

steps.body: Raisins contain more iron per calorie than do grapes?
steps.label: Why is it that

steps.body:
There must be something about the process of going from a grape to a raisin that increases the iron per calorie.
A ratio like Iron/Calorie can be increased two ways: increase the numerator (add more iron) or decrease the denominator (subtract calories).
The facts we're provided about the process of going from grape to raisin are these: - some sugar is caramelized - nothing is added - water evaporates (but water contains no calories)
steps.label: Evaluate

rows.stimulus: Raisins are made by drying grapes in the sun. Although some of the sugar in the grapes is caramelized in the process, nothing is added. Moreover, the only thing removed from the grapes is the water that evaporates during the drying, and water contains no calories or nutrients. The fact that raisins contain more iron per calorie than grapes do is thus puzzling.

rows.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes Rossi's argument?
rows.stimulus:
Rossi: It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented. So children should have the right to vote, since sometimes the interests of children are different from those of their parents.
Smith: Granted, children’s interests are not always the same as their parents’; governmental deficits incurred by their parents’ generation will later affect their own generation’s standard of living. But even if children are told about the issues affecting them, which is not generally the case, their conceptions of what can or should be done are too simple, and their time horizons are radically different from those of adults, so we cannot give them the responsibility of voting.

rows.prompt: The situation described above most closely conforms to which one of the following generalizations?
rows.stimulus: Among Trinidadians guppies, males with large spots are more attractive to females than are males with small spots, who consequently are presented with less frequent mating opportunities. Yet guppies with small spots are more likely to avoid detection by predators, so in waters where predators are abundant only guppies with small spots live to maturity.

choices.text: The government should not silence any group for advocating a position that a significant proportion of society believes to be beneficial.

One ought to advocate a position only if one believes that it is true or would be beneficial.

rows.prompt: Which one of the following principles most helps to justify the reasoning in the argument?
rows.stimulus: The government is being urged to prevent organizations devoted to certain views on human nutrition from advocating a diet that includes large portions of uncooked meat, because eating uncooked meat can be very dangerous. However, this purported fact does not justify the government's silencing the groups, for surely the government would not be justified in silencing a purely political group merely on the grounds that the policies the group advocates could be harmful to some members of society. The same should be true for silencing groups with certain views on human nutrition.

choices.text: Several similar experiments using older children and adults found that these subjects, too, had a general tendency to pay more attention to octaves, fifths, and fourths than to other musical intervals.
None of the babies in the experiment had previous exposure to music from any culture.

Octaves, fifths, and fourths were played more frequently during the experiment than other musical intervals were.

rows.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
rows.stimulus: In an experiment, researchers played a series of musical intervals—two-note sequences—to a large, diverse group of six-month-old babies. They found that the babies paid significantly more attention when the intervals were perfect octaves, fifths, or fourths than otherwise. These intervals are prevalent in the musical systems of most cultures around the world. Thus, humans probably have a biological predisposition to pay more attention to those intervals than to others.

rows.body:
This isn't a true paradox. Nothing here is surprising. The stem just wants explanations for a drop in the number of bass caught.

Think about what "number of bass caught" depends on. It takes two things: bass in the water and people fishing for them. So there are two roads to fewer bass caught:
1. **Fewer bass downstream.** They died, got eaten, moved away, or lost their habitat.
2. **Less fishing downstream.** Fewer anglers, or anglers fishing less.

Expect most of the answers we eliminate to come in on road 1, with at least one sneaking in on road 2.

Most students only think of road 1, because the wastewater feels like it must be hurting the fish. But road 2 is just as good. If half the anglers stop showing up, half as many bass get caught, even if the bass are thriving.
rows.label: Evaluate

rows.body:
Eliminate four answers that explain fewer bass caught, by either road. The correct answer will do neither, or it will push the other way: more bass or more fishing, which should mean *more* bass caught.

Be careful with any answer about anglers. It isn't out of scope. Anglers are half the equation.
